name: Moore's Law
title: Gordon Moore publishes "Cramming more components onto integrated circuits"
text: Writing in Electronics magazine, Moore observed that the number of components on an integrated circuit had doubled every year and predicted the trend would continue; in 1975 he revised the pace to every two years. It was a forecast about economics and manufacturing, not a law of physics, and it became the industry's planning target.

name: Intel 4004
title: The first commercial microprocessor ships
text: Intel's 4004 put a complete 4-bit processor on one chip with about 2,300 transistors, built for a Busicom calculator. Every point on the transistor line descends from it. The Apollo Guidance Computer that landed on the Moon two years earlier used integrated circuits carrying a few transistors each.

name: Backpropagation
title: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams publish the backpropagation paper in Nature
text: "Learning representations by back-propagating errors" made it practical to train multi-layer neural networks. The method was known earlier, but this paper is the one that spread it. Training compute for neural networks in the Epoch dataset starts climbing steadily after it.

name: Deep Blue
title: IBM's Deep Blue defeats Garry Kasparov
text: A purpose-built chess machine beat the world champion in a six-game match. It searched positions by brute force rather than learning, which is why it sits off the training-compute line, but it fixed in public memory the idea that raw computation could reach a human peak.

name: GeForce 256
title: NVIDIA ships the GeForce 256 and coins the term GPU
text: A chip built to draw video-game triangles in parallel. Its descendants became the hardware that trains every model on this page: the same massively parallel arithmetic that shades pixels also multiplies the matrices inside a neural network.

name: CUDA
title: NVIDIA releases CUDA 1.0
text: CUDA let programmers run general computation on graphics chips without disguising it as graphics. It turned the GPU from a gaming part into the default engine for scientific computing and, five years later, deep learning.

name: AlexNet
title: AlexNet wins the ImageNet competition
text: A deep convolutional network trained on two consumer GPUs cut the ImageNet error rate by roughly ten points over the best conventional method. It is the usual start date for the deep-learning era, and this page indexes the growth comparison to 2012 for that reason. AI training compute begins doubling every six months or so from here.

name: AlphaGo
title: AlphaGo defeats Lee Sedol 4–1
text: DeepMind's Go program beat one of the strongest players alive in a game long considered out of reach for computers. Unlike Deep Blue it learned, from human games and then from self-play, and its successors dropped the human games entirely.

name: Transformer
title: "Attention Is All You Need" introduces the Transformer
text: A Google architecture that replaced recurrence with attention and, crucially, scaled well on parallel hardware. Nearly every large model since, including every GPT, Claude, Gemini and Llama, is a Transformer. The architecture is what let training compute keep converting into capability.

name: Scaling laws
title: Kaplan et al. publish "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models"
text: The paper showed that language-model loss falls as a smooth power law in compute, data and parameters across many orders of magnitude. It gave labs a reason to believe that spending more compute would keep paying off, which is the belief the training-compute line records.

name: GPT-3
title: OpenAI publishes GPT-3, 175 billion parameters
text: Trained with roughly 3×10²³ FLOP, GPT-3 was about ten times larger than any previous language model and could perform tasks from a few examples in its prompt. It is the point at which parameter counts for frontier models stopped being routinely published a few years later.

name: ChatGPT
title: OpenAI releases ChatGPT
text: A chat interface on a GPT-3.5 model reached an estimated hundred million users within two months. Nothing on the compute axis changes that day; what changed was demand, and the training-compute frontier steepens through 2023 and 2024 as labs raced to follow.

name: Blackwell
title: NVIDIA announces the Blackwell GPU, 208 billion transistors
text: Two reticle-limit dies joined into one 208-billion-transistor package, the largest count on the transistor line when announced. Cerebras's wafer-scale WSE-3, at roughly four trillion transistors, is a single wafer rather than a chip and is left off the line for that reason.

name: o1: reasoning models
title: OpenAI previews o1, the first "reasoning" model
text: o1 was trained to think through a problem before answering and to spend more compute at inference time. Benchmark frontiers bend upward from this point: the math and science panels below jump within months, and the METR task-horizon series accelerates.

name: DeepSeek-R1
title: DeepSeek releases R1 with open weights
text: A Chinese lab published a reasoning model comparable to o1, with weights anyone could download, and reported a training budget far below what Western labs were assumed to spend. It made open-weight Chinese models a permanent feature of the frontier and prompted a brief market panic over compute demand.

name: Humanity's Last Exam
title: Humanity's Last Exam is published
text: Roughly three thousand expert-written questions across more than a hundred subjects, built specifically because earlier benchmarks had saturated. Frontier models scored under ten percent at release. It is the last panel below that has not been solved.
